articles.title: Arab parties score historic win in Israel polls, putting Netanyahu's hopes at risk
articles.summary: Arab political parties have emerged as a major force in Israel's election, securing a record number of seats and leaving both Prime Minister Benjamin
articles.body: Arab political parties have emerged as a major force in Israel's election, securing a record number of seats and leaving both Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc and the opposition camp led by Gadi Eisenkot short of the numbers needed to form a government.With more than 85 per cent of votes counted, preliminary results on Wednesday gave Netanyahu's bloc 53 seats, compared with 48 for Eisenkot's bloc. Arab parties were projected to win a historic 19 seats in the 120-member Knesset, where 61 seats are required for a majority. The results were not final, with votes still to be counted.The strong showing follows an unusually high turnout among Arab voters, many of whom had previously stayed away from national elections. Arab citizens make up around 20 per cent of Israel's population, and the campaign saw growing mobilisation amid anger over the government's policies and concerns about racism and discrimination.In towns such as Majd al-Krum in northern Israel, turnout reached 85 per cent of eligible voters. The result has given Arab lawmakers greater potential influence over the formation of the next government, although it remains uncertain whether the opposition will agree to rely on their support.Netanyahu's Likud alleges election was stolenAs the results showed no clear path to a majority for either main bloc, Netanyahu's Likud party alleged that Arab parties had manipulated the election and demanded an investigation into alleged voter fraud."The elections in the State of Israel were stolen by Arab parties that support terrorism and the elimination of the Jewish state through serious criminal offences of bribery, threats, violence, forgeries, and the use of prohibited software to mobilise voters," the party said in a statement shared by Netanyahu on X.Likud claimed it was submitting hundreds of testimonies and other pieces of evidence to the police, the Shin Bet domestic security agency and the Central Elections Committee. It cited alleged cash payments to voters, threats against polling officials, multiple voting and discrepancies in ballot records."We demand from the police and the Shin Bet a thorough investigation into the election theft by the Arab parties and the full prosecution of the criminals," Likud said.The party also called on the Central Elections Committee to investigate the allegations before the results were finalised, describing the alleged offences as "a serious blow to Israeli democracy and the voting rights of Israeli citizens".These claims have not been established as fact. An official from the Central Elections Committee had earlier dismissed claims of widespread fraud, according to Israeli media reports.Will Arab parties help the opposition form a governmentThe election has left both main camps facing a difficult task. Netanyahu's bloc remains short of the 61 seats needed for a majority, while Eisenkot's opposition bloc also cannot reach that threshold without support from parties outside its current grouping.Yair Golan, leader of the Democrats party, has urged the opposition to work with the Arab-led Joint List and Ra'am parties to replace Netanyahu. The Joint List has also indicated it is ready to help pave the way for Netanyahu's removal.However, forming such an arrangement could prove difficult. Netanyahu has repeatedly opposed a government that depends on Arab parties, while some opposition leaders have also been reluctant to enter an alliance with them.The Arab parties' record performance has therefore made them potentially decisive in negotiations, but it does not guarantee that they will join a governing coalition. With counting continuing and no bloc holding a majority, Israel faces potentially prolonged negotiations over who will lead its next government.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Meet Ryan Ragsdale, the 11-year-old Texas boy who sold 700 Pokémon cards, childhood toys and hand-painted rocks, turning six years of school fundraising into more than $20,000 for heart research and outreach
articles.summary: An 11-year-old schoolboy from Texas has given away hundreds of his own toys, Pokémon cards and hand-painted rocks over six years.
articles.body: An 11-year-old schoolboy from Texas has given away hundreds of his own toys, Pokémon cards and hand-painted rocks over six years. He has raised more than $20,000 for children born with heart defects. Ryan Ragsdale is a fifth-grade pupil at Lorena Elementary School. He first joined the American Heart Association’s Kids Heart Challenge at age five, when he was in kindergarten. He came home wanting to help “kids with holes in their hearts.” He worked out a plan with his mother to sell his own childhood things instead of just asking neighbours for cash. Data released by the American Heart Association confirms that Ryan’s yearly toy sales have raised more than $20,000 (£15,800) for the charity’s medical research, public education and health advocacy campaigns. Every February, Ryan clears out his bedroom to find items to list for local buyers. Over six years, he has sold about 700 Pokémon cards from his own collection. He has also sold a Thomas the Tank Engine train set and a Jurassic Park-era Tyrannosaurus Rex toy that he had kept since he was three years old.Raising money by selling childhood treasuresThe idea for the yearly sale began when Ryan asked his mother, Sarah Ragsdale-Kline, how he could make a bigger difference through his school’s fundraising drive. “He decided he would give up toys he still loved because he wanted other kids to have healthy hearts like his,” Sarah Ragsdale-Kline told the American Heart Association Newsroom. “He’s always been friendly and never met a stranger, but the passion he had at such a young age to help others was something remarkable.” According to the charity’s local news release, Ryan’s biggest single sale was a family pitching machine that sold for $50. He also sold a garden swing set. Relatives, neighbours and family friends gave him items too, because they wanted to support his fundraising. To raise more money, Ryan collects stones and paints them. He uses designs he finds online or ones inspired by the natural shape of each stone. Every buyer of an item or a rock gets a joke from Ryan. His mother buys him an age-appropriate joke book each year. It is part of a family rule that “laughing is good for the heart.” Ryan said his favorite joke this year is: “What makes a tooth fairy so smart? Wisdom teeth.”Celebrating a six-year milestoneRyan looked back on his six years of fundraising. He said his favourite part of each sale is counting up the final cash total with his mother at the end. “I feel really proud and excited that I’m making a difference,” Ryan told the American Heart Association. His mother said Ryan sets a higher target for himself every year. He clearly understands where the money goes. “Every year, he sets a higher goal than the year before,” Sarah Ragsdale-Kline said. “He does it because he knows the money is going to kids who need it.” Lorena Elementary School plans to honour Ryan’s efforts at a special school assembly on 27 March, according to the American Heart Association. Outside of his charity work, Ryan already has his sights set on a career in law. “I like debating with people about what I think the correct answer would be,” Ryan said. “I can go on and on about why I was right.” His mother added that his debate skills are already well known at home. “He keeps us on our toes,” Sarah Ragsdale-Kline said. “But truly, it’s an honor to be his mom. The amazing things he does and the heart behind it all inspire us every year.”How school fundraising supports heart researchThe Kids Heart Challenge is a service-learning program run by the American Heart Association in primary and secondary schools across the United States. According to the organisation, money raised through the nationwide school program pays for scientific research into congenital heart defects. It also funds community health programmes. It teaches pupils life-saving skills, such as Hands-Only CPR and healthy eating habits. Schools that take part, such as Lorena Elementary, also get financial give-backs and equipment credits based on the total money their pupils raise. This helps physical education departments buy new sports and fitness gear.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: What is happening with US interest rates?
articles.summary: The Federal Reserve's interest rate decisions affect everything from mortgages to car loans
articles.body:
The US Federal Reserve has held interest rates steady at 3.75% - 4%.

The decision comes within a week of the midterm elections and after the central bank raised interest rates for the first time in three years at its September meeting.

"The overwhelming consensus, the overwhelming judgement, is that what we've done in this monetary medicine is starting to work some," Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said, referring to September's interest rate rise.

An interest rate tells people and businesses how much it costs to borrow money – such as with credit cards, mortgages, or business loans – but also what return they get for saving cash.

The Fed influences interest rates in the US through its target range for the federal funds rate, which is the interest rate used by commercial banks for overnight borrowing.

What's happening with US interest rates?

In its decision to hold rates steady this month, the Fed said that while inflation remains high, it wanted to gather more information before making another decision to change rates.

The Fed also noted that while there was uncertainty, the US economy remained resilient.

Warsh acknowledged that inflation remained too high, but noted that there were other signs - such as tightening credit conditions - that the economy was moving in the right direction.

There is plenty more economic data to come between now and the committee's next meeting, the Fed chair added, which should paint a more detailed picture of the state of the economy.

At that point, Warsh said, "we'll be, I think, better positioned to determine the right policy decision and the stance of policy."

While last month the committee signalled there could be one more rate rise this year, Warsh would not be drawn out on where he thinks they will go in six weeks' time.

"A lot of things can happen, so I'm not going to be able to share with you my musings."

The decision to hold rates steady was not unanimous.

While 10 of the 12 committee members voted to keep rates unchanged, Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack voted to increase rates to 4%-4.25%, from its current 3.75%-4%.

The bank's next meeting will be held over 8-9 December.

How does the Fed rate affect mortgages, credit cards, and savings?

The Fed uses interest rate changes to try to keep inflation – the rate at which prices change – at 2% a year and keep the job market stable.

When inflation is too high, the Fed tends to raise interest rates.

This tends to mean higher rates from banks and other lenders, which in turn affects spending and saving decisions.

For example, someone refinancing their mortgage or buying a property for the first time could face higher mortgage rates. It could also mean higher interest rates on credit cards or car loans. However, it means higher interest rates on savings as well.

This encourages people and businesses to save more, spend less money, and make less investments. It also encourages companies to hire less people or slow the pace of pay rises.

All of this tends to reduce demand and slow inflation.

When inflation is low or if the Fed believes the economy needs a boost, it cut rates.

The idea is that this will have the opposite affect, with banks dropping rates leading to more spending and less saving from people and businesses.

Leaving the rates unchanged means rates on things like new mortgages or business loans are also less likely to change. It also means interest rates on cash savings are unlikely to rise.

How much have US interest rates changed?

US interest rates have historically moved around quite a bit.

The last time Fed rates were as high as they have been recently was in the lead up to and during the start of the 2008 global financial crisis.

The Fed then dropped rates to historic lows to encourage spending and job creation during the economic slump and kept them at those lows for several years.

They picked up again ahead of the pandemic before dropping to as low as 0%-0.25% during the pandemic. They then rose to highs of 5.25%-5% from the middle of 2023 to August 2024 as inflation jumped.

They had been falling steadily since then, until rates were raised last month.

articles.title: In 2008, Angelina Jolie co-founded KIND with Microsoft; it has since secured legal representation for over 17,000 children in the US and supported migrant families
articles.summary: Aryad, 16, had fled conflict in Africa and reached the Polish border alone. He had just completed a dangerous journey and was traumatised.
articles.body: Aryad, 16, had fled conflict in Africa and reached the Polish border alone. He had just completed a dangerous journey and was traumatised. Unfamiliar with the asylum procedure, he was at risk of being returned to danger. His future looked uncertain.This is the kind of case Kids in Need of Defense, known as KIND, was established to address. According to the organisation, a lawyer from its network stepped in, helped establish that the boy was an unaccompanied child and secured his placement in foster care. The lawyer stayed with the child throughout the asylum process. "Aryad is now rebuilding his life and pursuing vocational training," the NGO said in its July 2026 report.“At KIND, we do this work for kids who made their dangerous journey to safety alone in hopes of one day living a more secure future filled with promise,” Wendy Young, KIND’s president, said.Angelina Jolie joined hands with MicrosoftIn 2008, Microsoft and Angelina Jolie, who is now listed as the organisation’s co-founder and patron, established KIND, an NGO devoted to protecting unaccompanied and separated children.Children who arrived in the United States without a parent often faced immigration court proceedings alone, in a language they barely spoke, with no one to explain what was happening to them. KIND connects children with pro bono attorneys from law firms, corporations, law schools and bar associations. During its first year, KIND opened offices in seven US cities, including Baltimore, Maryland; Boston, Massachusetts; Houston, Texas; Los Angeles, California; New York, New York; and Washington, D.C.Since its founding in 2008, KIND has provided legal representation to more than 17,000 children in the US and educated over 78,000 children about their legal rights in the US and Mexico. Legal representation is only part of its work. KIND also runs psychosocial support programmes that connect children with support services. It has provided psychological support to more than 30,000 children and family members across the two countries. Medical care, mental health services, schooling and crisis support are also part of the organisation’s work. Many of the children it serves have lived through violence, and a lawyer alone cannot undo that.“Through a holistic approach, we combine legal services, advocacy, and partnerships across the private sector, philanthropy, government, and civil society to protect unaccompanied and separated children. We work to ensure that migration systems recognize these children first and foremost as children—supporting their rights through high-quality legal representation and services, child by child,” the organisation says.For children who arrive alone or have been separated from their parents, a lawyer can make the difference between being sent away and being heard. KIND’s website carries a testimonial from a former client, Erica, who describes her experience. “When we went to court, I never felt alone because I had a KIND representative by my side to help me with my case.” Erica’s words pretty much sum up what the organisation’s work is meant to achieve. Immigration court can be intimidating for adults, and it is far harder for a child who does not speak the language and has no family in the room.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Billionaire Clara Wu Tsai backed the New York Liberty’s rise to a $600 million franchise and pledged $50 million to Brooklyn communities; now her latest plan targets new mothers
articles.summary: Billionaire Clara Wu Tsai has helped transform the New York Liberty from a struggling basketball team into a franchise valued at $600 million, while
articles.body: Billionaire Clara Wu Tsai has helped transform the New York Liberty from a struggling basketball team into a franchise valued at $600 million, while directing millions of dollars towards social and economic initiatives in Brooklyn. Now, her philanthropic work is turning towards new mothers in Brownsville, where a proposed guaranteed income programme aims to provide direct financial support to families. The initiative forms part of a $50 million commitment she made with her husband, Alibaba co-founder Joe Tsai, in 2020. Alongside investments in sport, education and small businesses, the plan adds another dimension to Wu Tsai’s efforts to expand economic opportunities across Brooklyn.How Clara Wu Tsai built her role in BrooklynWu Tsai occupies several positions across sport, entertainment and philanthropy. She is vice chair of Brooklyn Sports & Entertainment, the organisation behind the Brooklyn Nets, the New York Liberty and Barclays Center, and serves as governor of the Liberty. Her interests also extend to film production, including Werner Herzog's Bucking Fastard, which premiered at the Venice Film Festival in September 2026. She co-owns the San Diego Seals, a National Lacrosse League team, and holds trustee positions at Stanford University, NewYork-Presbyterian Hospital and Lincoln Center.Her work in Brooklyn took on a different dimension in August 2020. During a period of racial justice protests, she and her husband, Alibaba co-founder Joe Tsai, announced a $50 million commitment over 10 years for social justice and economic mobility initiatives, with Brooklyn as the principal focus.How Clara Wu Tsai plans to support new mothers in BrownsvilleThe Social Justice Fund has earmarked money for a guaranteed income initiative aimed at new mothers in the neighbourhood, according to reporting by the New York Times cited in October 2026.Under this model, selected recipients receive regular cash payments without being required to spend the money on specific items or meet conventional work-related conditions. The approach differs from universal basic income, which would extend payments to a much wider population. For families adjusting to the arrival of a child, unrestricted financial assistance can be used according to individual needs, including household expenses and costs associated with caring for a baby.New York City has already tested related approaches. The Bridge Project, a non-profit organisation, has run a cash assistance programme for expectant mothers, while the city has also explored guaranteed income through other initiatives. The Brownsville programme is still short on publicly available details. Its planned scale, payment amounts and launch date have not been disclosed, leaving questions about how many families might participate and how the scheme will operate.Loans and support for Brooklyn businessesSmall businesses were among the first beneficiaries of the fund's economic mobility work. In 2021, it introduced EXCELerate, offering low-interest and interest-free loans to businesses dealing with the effects of the pandemic. The programme was intended to help owners reopen, maintain operations or recover from a difficult trading period.In March 2026, the fund also joined the Asian American Foundation, Renaissance Economic Development Corporation and New York State in a $5.5 million small-business lending initiative. Such arrangements place the fund alongside other organisations providing capital to businesses that may struggle to obtain financing through conventional channels.The organisation has also backed early-stage companies. Its BK-XL accelerator, developed with Boston-based Visible Hands, invested more than $4 million in 17 startups led by founders of colour.Brooklyn basketball courts, arts programmes and questions over the fund’s impactThe fund has put money into neighbourhood projects beyond business financing. Working with NYC Parks, it says it has renovated 12 basketball courts across four Brooklyn parks. The locations include East New York, Flatlands, Crown Heights and Sunset Park, areas where gun violence has been a concern. The court improvements form part of an initiative costing roughly $2 million.Arts education is another strand of the programme. Its school projects draw on the work of Brooklyn-born artist Jean-Michel Basquiat and jazz musician Max Roach, connecting their legacies with music and arts curricula in public schools. Wu Tsai has also used Barclays Center as a venue for free community events, including summer concerts on the arena plaza. Brooklyn journalist Norman Oder, who has followed the arena and its development for around two decades, has examined the fund's public reporting and raised concerns about how its spending and claimed impact can be independently assessed.Among the figures he challenged was the number of students reached by the Basquiat programme. After Oder questioned the original estimate of 70,000, the fund revised it to 12,000. He has also reported that tax filings for the Joe and Clara Tsai Foundation list no grants and argued that the fund does not provide a complete public accounting of its expenditure. The fund has told him that administrative costs account for 10% of its money.The investment that changed the New York LibertyWu Tsai's sporting career has been closely tied to the fortunes of the Liberty. The team was previously owned by Madison Square Garden chairman James Dolan, who moved it away from the Garden in 2018 to the Westchester County Center in White Plains. The venue had a capacity of roughly 5,000, a substantial change for a franchise associated with New York's largest sporting arena.Joe and Clara Tsai acquired the Liberty in January 2019 and brought the team to Barclays Center the following season. Wu Tsai has since spoken about the importance of giving women's basketball players resources comparable to those available to male athletes. In an interview with Vanity Fair, she described the players as highly capable athletes whose opportunities had not always reflected their talent.The ownership group made several investments that attracted attention across the WNBA. In 2021, the Tsais arranged charter flights for Liberty players, an expense that resulted in a record $500,000 league fine at the time. Charter flights have since become standard across the league, reflecting a wider change in how teams handle player travel.The franchise is also developing a new practice facility in Greenpoint, Brooklyn. The $80 million project is scheduled to open in 2027. Part of its financing came through the sale of a minority stake in the team at a then-record valuation of $450 million.The financial figures have moved sharply since the acquisition. The Tsais paid a reported $10 million to $14 million for the franchise, while Sportico valued it at $600 million in 2026. Wu Tsai has said she hopes to build the Liberty into a billion-dollar team, a target that would place it among the most valuable franchises in women's sport.The Golden State Valkyries have already reached that mark. CNBC valued the WNBA team at $1 billion in 2026, giving the Liberty ownership group a recent example of how quickly valuations in the league can rise.The foundation behind the projectsThe Social Justice Fund operates as an initiative of the Joe and Clara Tsai Foundation, which the couple established together. Joe Tsai is the co-founder and chairman of Alibaba Group, the Chinese technology and e-commerce company. The foundation's activities sit alongside the couple's investments in professional sport and other areas of philanthropy.Their personal circumstances changed in late July 2026, when they announced that they were divorcing. They said the separation would not alter their respective positions within Brooklyn Sports & Entertainment and the teams. Joe Tsai would remain chairman of the organisation and governor of the Nets, while Clara Wu Tsai would continue as vice chair and governor of the Liberty.The announcement did not change the public plans associated with the Social Justice Fund, including its proposed work with new mothers. The fund's original $50 million commitment spans a decade, although public reporting has raised questions about the full accounting of its spending and the measurement of its results.Scientific research and the next set of ambitionsWu Tsai's interests also include human performance research. In 2021, she and Joe Tsai committed $220 million to the Wu Tsai Human Performance Alliance, a collaboration involving six universities and anchored at Stanford. The initiative studies elite athletes and human performance, with the broader aim of applying findings to health and wellbeing beyond professional sport.Wu Tsai has described her ambitions for Liberty and scientific research as goals she does not want to choose between. Asked by Fortune earlier in 2026 whether she would prefer to build a billion-dollar basketball franchise or achieve a major scientific discovery, she said she wanted both.You use AI every day. articles.title: FBI reports 67% jump in violent crime arrests under Trump compared to Biden’s final months
articles.summary: Kash Patel says the FBI arrested over 47,000 violent criminals and gang members in 21 months, marking a 67% increase over the Biden era.
articles.body: The FBI has made significant gains in combating crime and arresting violent offenders and child predators over the past 21 months under the Trump administration, according to data released by the agency on Wednesday. In that timeframe, the FBI arrested more than 47, 000 violent criminals and gang members — a 67% increase compared to the final 21 months of the Biden administration. Arrests of child sex predators and human traffickers also rose 13%, reaching just over 6,000, agency figures show. articles.title: Andy Burnham rules out early general election in next 12 months
articles.summary: The prime minister has denied speculation from some opposition parties that he will go to the country in spring 2027.
articles.body:
Andy Burnham has ruled out an early general election in the next 12 months, after opposition parties suggested one would be called.

The next UK general election must be held by August 2029, and there has been speculation that the prime minister is preparing for an earlier poll.

Asked directly if he would call a snap election within the next year, the prime minister told broadcasters: "I don't know how many times I've done this now but yes, I can rule out calling a general election in the next 12 months."

He said he was focusing on people over the Labour Party, adding: "I'm not thinking about myself. I'm not thinking about my own party and its prospects."

Earlier this month, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch suggested Burnham may go to the country early.

She said the Conservative Party was "coming back" after it slumped in popularity at the end of 14 years in government, telling BBC South East: "This is an era of political volatility and multi-party politics."

She added: "I do think Andy Burnham is going to call an election sooner than he is saying... all the policies he announced are for after an election."

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said in September he believed there would be an election "next spring".

"I believe there must be a general election because Andy Burnham has no mandate - the messiah without a mandate, we deserve a general election on who continues to govern this country."

Burnham was elected MP in June after the Makerfield by-election, before securing the Labour Party leadership and becoming prime minister after Sir Keir Starmer lost the support of Labour MPs and quit Downing Street.

He has since outlined a number of ambitions , which has led some to question whether he will try to secure a fresh mandate before 2029.

One of these issues is Brexit, where Burnham has said he wants an "honest conversation" about the UK's future relationship with the EU.

On Wednesday, he promised to stick to the red lines in his party's 2024 manifesto on EU freedom of movement, the single market and customs union "for the whole of this Parliament".

The current Parliamentary term runs until the next general election.

Burnham has repeatedly denied he is seeking a snap poll. He told broadcasters on Wednesday: "We've got a 10-year plan to come, and that will inform the spending review next year. These are my priorities, not looking at our own internal party political advantage."

articles.title: An Ohio woman bought a 4,000-square-foot church for $1; she put $75,000 into structural repairs before completing the conversion
articles.summary: Discover how Taylor Abbott turned a dilapidated church in Clarington, Ohio, purchased for just $1, into a stunning modern residence after investing $75,000 in essential structural repairs.
articles.body: When Taylor Abbott was given the opportunity to purchase a structure that had previously united a small community for just $1, it was in danger of being demolished. The declining congregation in Clarington, Ohio, could no longer afford to maintain the dilapidated church. Abbott and his spouse, Alexandra, made the decision to preserve the structure and make it their residence. Although it cost very little to buy, it took a lot of labour to make the building safe and habitable. Before obtaining funding to finish the conversion, Abbott paid $75,000 of his own money for structural repairs. The couple eventually moved into the former Church of Christ in June 2019, about three years after acquiring it. The renovation preserved much of the building's original appearance while introducing the living spaces needed for a modern home.A $1 purchase with serious problemsThe Clarington Church of Christ was dedicated in October of 1906. By 2016, attendance had dropped down to only a few ageing members who could no longer afford to keep the place up. The church was confronted with a tough dilemma: locate someone prepared to assume ownership of the property or pay to have the structure dismantled. The local church had a member approach the town council about donating the structure, but officials felt it was too much of a problem. Then she called the Abbotts, who had experience with renovations of older properties.Taylor turned the idea down at first. But the day after driving past the church, he changed his mind and arranged to see it. He was intrigued by old structures, but the state of this one made the size of the undertaking instantly obvious. Inside, the church had water-damaged ceilings, blue carpet, old woodwork and floors that had buckled over the years. Roof leaks and windows needing restoration were added to the list of fixes. The attic also included original oak rafters and a gorgeous tin ceiling concealed under a later suspended ceiling.The most serious problem was in the basement. A large crack ran through the foundation wall, and the structure had shifted roughly a foot out of position. Water, leaves and debris had entered through the damaged area, and the walls above showed the effects. Despite the problems, Abbott agreed to buy the church. When he asked how much the remaining congregation wanted, a member suggested $1 because demolition alone was estimated to cost about $10,000. Abbott’s first-person story of the purchase and restoration was published by Weelunk. This was not only about getting an inexpensive place. It was about taking over a building that needed a lot of repair before it could be lived in.Structural repairs came firstThe couple had to deal with the foundation problem before they could worry about the inside. With hydraulic equipment and temporary supports, contractors lifted the building and removed the damaged piece of the foundation, replacing it with a strengthened wall with vertical steel beams. They even put in a French drain system to help divert water away from the structure.The work was expensive. Abbott put $75,000 of his money into the building to make sure it was structurally sound. That investment was significant for another reason, too: he required a lender willing to provide him a construction loan on the rest of the conversion. Financing an unusual property was not simple. The church didn’t have a typical kitchen and bedroom, which made it particularly challenging to obtain a conventional home construction loan. Some banks had stated that a commercial loan, with a higher rate of interest in most cases, could be the only alternative. After Abbott presented his designs for the final home, a local bank agreed to consider the proposal.The foundation construction also added an unanticipated problem. When the structure was lowered down on the rebuilt foundation, the floor was still slanted, about 12 inches variation in height from back to front. Several window apertures were not properly aligned with the windows. This meant the pair had to replace the entire floor, an unanticipated cost of $11,000. A new roof was put on, and the bell tower was repaired. The event demonstrates a perennial dilemma with the rehabilitation of historic buildings: correcting one structural fault can uncover others that were concealed or only visible once the building is stabilised.A 2004 Massachusetts Institute of Technology thesis on adaptive reuse of churches identified structural condition, financing, laws and the interests of numerous stakeholders as important factors in whether a former church may be successfully transformed to another use. The Abbott project at one time had its share of such problems.Keeping the church's characterThe next task after the structural work was to design a dwelling that functioned well but also retained the qualities that gave the church its character. Abbott drew up the new layout with the help of his wife and grandmother; relatives and friends helped with some of the demolition. The couple required a bedroom, bathroom and laundry, but Abbott was intent on keeping the high ceiling that had originally drawn his eye. The answer was an 825-square-foot loft, providing living space upstairs and room for a master suite downstairs. The rest of the floor was converted into an open-plan kitchen and living room.Some of the repair work was carried out by specialists. A preservation business refurbished the approximately 2,000-square-foot ornamental tin ceiling, and a local craftsman repaired the original windows. The woodwork, casings and trim were polished; the damaged outside siding was repaired and painted white. The outside was still recognisably a church, because the bell tower and historic architectural proportions were retained. The building’s big open layout and loft made it suitable as a house, yet it retained the ancient ceiling and other original characteristics.The move is part of a wider problem of church conservation. When congregations dwindle or migrate, structures erected for worship can be difficult to keep up, even if they remain essential to a community’s history. A 2012 University of Cincinnati thesis on holy building conversions explores the restoration and adaptation of sacred buildings to maintain their significance to a community while repurposing them. Abbott’s conversion had a personal tie to the building’s past, too. He found, when investigating his family history, that one of his ancestors, a Thaddeus Thomas, had helped build the church. The edifice was built of hardwood from neighbouring land, and the congregation consecrated the building the following year in 1905.That finding added another historical dimension to the endeavour. The family was converting a historic structure to modern demands but also maintaining a building which had a connection with the older inhabitants of the area. A 2022 research study on adaptive reuse in religious heritage structures analysed 65 international cases and showed that effective reuse is reliant on more than the architectural conversion. Decisions on the building's future use, heritage characteristics and relationship with the local community all affect the outcome.After three years of planning, restoration and repair work, the Abbotts moved into their home in June 2019. Three years later, when the property was finished, the local bank permitted them to convert their financing to a standard home mortgage. The $1 purchase was just the beginning. The $75,000 structural investment, foundation reconstruction, floor replacement and preservation work transformed a crumbling church into a working residence. Its interior has a different purpose, although its façade still resembles the structure dedicated in 1906. The conversion spared the church from demolition; it was structurally sound and ready for another generation of use.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: In 2012, a Texas landowner recounted tracing a company on his mother’s gas statement to drilling on the family farm; her first royalty check was $600,000, and payments later reached $40,000 a month
articles.summary: A Texas farmer's remarkable discovery of gas royalties changed his family's financial fate, revealing the hidden value of their land. Learn how a single tax statement led to $600,000 in initial revenue and ongoing monthly checks of $40,000.
articles.body: Something significantly more important than the amount owed can be found on a standard tax statement. A Texas landowner named Max Lindsey made a revelation that changed his family's financial situation after seeing a business name on his mother's documents. The family had not received much information about the potential value of their property, which had been subject to a gas drilling agreement for decades. Lindsey started phoning and looking into the business mentioned in the statement. He discovered that the mineral rights his parents had committed to lease many years prior were producing a sizable revenue and that gas was being produced from the family's land.His mother, Roberta Hudson Lindsey, received her first royalty check for $600,000. Max Lindsey's own largest monthly royalty payment later reached $40,000, according to a 2012 report by The News Outlet, republished by The Vindicator. The discovery brought substantial income to a family that had spent generations farming and raising cattle on the same property.The clue hidden in the paperworkLindsey was doing his mother’s taxes when he saw the name of a production business on an oil well tax statement. Rather than file it away in the cabinet, he went online, found the company's manufacturing office and called them. The answer was that his parents had signed a contract in the mid-20th century allowing gas drilling on their farm. For decades, the deal had yielded no apparent financial advantage because drilling never commenced. The family continued to farm and raise cattle, at times having difficulty meeting household bills.The family owned 170 acres near Rhome, Texas, and had held the property since 1850. According to the 2012 report, Lindsey's relatives settled in Texas after mining for gold during the California Gold Rush. The account does not specify exactly when they made the journey or when they acquired the land. Despite owning the property, the family had limited cash, and Lindsey's father once drove a school bus to supplement the household income. His mother maintained a garden and canned food for family meals. The contrast between these financial difficulties and the later royalty payments was striking. The money began flowing roughly a decade before Lindsey told the story in 2012, when his mother was already in her 80s. She was getting checks in the mail, he continued, but she didn’t quite understand what they meant.Why an old gas lease became valuableThe family’s experience came during the fast expansion of natural gas resources in north central Texas. Their territory was part of the larger area affected by the Barnett Shale, a geological formation that grew to be vital to the U.S. natural gas industry. The Railroad Commission of Texas's overview of the Barnett Shale describes it as one of the country's major onshore natural gas fields. The productive formation extends across thousands of square miles and includes Wise County, where the Lindsey property was located.The commercial emergence of shale gas has altered the economic value of numerous assets. Companies acquired the technology and the experience to produce gas from deposits that had previously been difficult or uneconomic to develop at scale. The U.S. Energy Information Administration's explanation of shale gas production identifies the Barnett Shale as a major starting point for large scale commercial shale gas production around 2000. As extraction techniques improved, companies expanded drilling across the region.For landowners who had held on to their mineral rights, the move might bring revenue from minerals beneath property they’d owned for decades. The value depended on the presence of a productive formation under the property, on whether operators developed it, and on what percentage of production the lease gave to the owners. Most of the wells on his family’s land were producing at 12.5% for them, Lindsey added. Some later leases signed by family had an 18.75% royalty. Those percentages were significant since a royalty owner’s payment is tied to the terms of the agreement and the volume and value of the gas generated.The money came with uncertaintyThe checks could be big, but Lindsey didn’t think of them as a sure wage. He'd retired from his work as a machinist at Lockheed Martin around 10 years ago and was also on Social Security. His wife still worked three days a week at a bank. "My biggest monthly payment was $40,000," he added, but he was careful not to structure his normal spending around revenue that may fluctuate. The production companies regulated the amount taken from the wells. Changes in the price of natural gas affected the value of the production and thus the royalty payments. Prices decreased, and operators cut back on production. The family’s monthly income dropped. A productive well could generate substantial royalty income during one period and much less during another.The Railroad Commission of Texas guide to oil and gas royalties explains that royalty records can include production volumes, prices, taxes, deductions and the owner's share of the proceeds. These details help explain why payments vary and why landowners need to understand the terms of their leases rather than judging income from a single check.The land itself had also changed. Lindsey said the amount of drilling made the property difficult to farm as it once had been. He continued raising cattle for meat, but the family could no longer rely on the same combination of crop production and livestock that had sustained earlier generations. Mineral rights became a valuable asset that buyers sought to acquire. Lindsey said his family received offers to buy those rights almost every week, including mailings involving sums of millions of dollars. He said he shredded some of the checks sent to him because he did not want to surrender future income without fully understanding the consequences.A windfall built on generations of ownershipLindsey advised other landowners to negotiate rather than accept the first offer they received. Lease terms can determine the royalty percentage, well locations, surface access and other conditions that affect the owner's interests for years. His family's experience also illustrates why landowners need to understand that ownership of the surface and ownership of the minerals beneath it can be separate. The value of mineral rights can change when new drilling technology makes previously inaccessible resources commercially viable.The family’s financial metamorphosis started not with a new investment or purchase, but with a company name on a tax statement. Taking that clue, Lindsey discovered an old drilling agreement for a resource that became valuable decades after the initial deal was made. The initial cheque for $600,000 and the ensuing monthly payments of up to $40,000 transformed the family’s situation, but the income was not guaranteed to remain at the same level. The production, the price of gas and the terms of the leases are what made the land yield what it did.For Lindsey, the discovery showed that a property's value can extend beyond what is visible at ground level. His family had farmed and raised cattle on the land for generations before gas production created a new source of income. The royalties also changed how the family could use the property and plan for the future.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: After losing his mother to a stroke at 58, Jack Buckley ran 58 half-marathons in 58 days and raised more than $30,000; a second endurance challenge brought in another $12,000
articles.summary: A son’s effort to honour his late mother has earned national recognition in Australia, after two demanding running challenges raised more than $42,000 for
articles.body: A son’s effort to honour his late mother has earned national recognition in Australia, after two demanding running challenges raised more than $42,000 for stroke awareness and support. According to the Stroke Foundation and regional news outlet Region Illawarra, Wollongong resident Jack Buckley has been named Fundraiser of the Year at the 2026 National Stroke Awards for turning personal loss into a campaign aimed at helping other families affected by stroke. Buckley lost his mother, Keryn, in February 2025, when she was just 58. Her death inspired him to take on an endurance challenge that would match her age with the number of races he completed, transforming a deeply personal tribute into a wider fundraising effort.58 half-marathons in 58 daysIn August 2025, Buckley began his challenge, known as 58 for You, setting out to run 58 half-marathons over 58 consecutive days. Each run represented one year of his mother’s life, with the goal of raising money for the Stroke Foundation and increasing awareness of the condition. The challenge covered more than 1,200 kilometres and tested him through difficult weather, physical exhaustion and the strain of maintaining such an intense schedule. He completed the final run on October 6, 2025, raising more than $30,000. The campaign was initially intended to raise $20,000, but the final total surpassed that target. The achievement also brought attention to the impact of sudden stroke on families and the importance of recognising that the condition can affect people who appear otherwise healthy.A second challenge lasting 58 hoursBuckley returned to fundraising in June 2026 with another endurance effort, choosing a format that reflected the same number at the centre of his original tribute. This time, he ran repeated loops over 58 hours, covering approximately 6.8 kilometres per circuit, with short breaks to rest and refuel. The challenge took place in the year his mother would have turned 60, adding another personal milestone to the effort. The second event raised a further $12,000, bringing the combined total from his two challenges to more than $42,000. Family members, friends and supporters helped sustain him through the difficult stretches, particularly when fatigue made continuing harder. The fundraising effort also encouraged conversations about stroke prevention, recovery and the support available to survivors and their families.National recognition for his effortsBuckley’s work was recognised at the 2026 National Stroke Awards, held in Melbourne on October 15. The awards celebrate people who have contributed to Australia’s stroke community, including survivors, carers, researchers, health professionals, volunteers and fundraisers. The Fundraiser of the Year category recognises individuals whose efforts go beyond ordinary fundraising to support the wider stroke community. Buckley’s achievement stood out for combining substantial fundraising with a sustained effort to improve public awareness. According to the Stroke Foundation, his campaign has helped hundreds of Australians learn more about stroke prevention and the warning signs that can require urgent medical attention. His fundraising journey is not over. Buckley is set to continue supporting the cause in 2027 as part of the Stroke Foundation’s London Marathon team, extending his commitment beyond the two challenges already completed.Turning personal loss into a wider missionStroke can affect not only the person experiencing it but also their families, who may suddenly find themselves facing life-changing medical decisions and an uncertain future. Awareness of warning signs and timely medical care are important parts of reducing the impact of stroke, while survivors and their loved ones may need ongoing support during recovery.For Buckley, the fundraising campaign has become a way to honour his mother while helping other families access information and support. His two challenges have demonstrated how a personal tribute can develop into a sustained public effort, with the money raised contributing to the Stroke Foundation’s work in prevention, awareness and recovery. The award recognises more than the distance he has covered or the funds he has collected. It acknowledges a campaign built around one family’s loss, with the aim of helping others understand stroke and reducing the number of families who experience a similar tragedy.You use AI every day. articles.title: DAVID MARCUS: In Dallas, Talarico’s firewall is starting to show some real cracks
articles.summary: James Talarico faces lagging Black voter enthusiasm and suburban skepticism in Dallas, where he needs massive numbers to offset Ken Paxton's rural edge.
articles.body: I met Mark, in his late 50s, at an upscale restaurant in downtown Dallas. He is a lifelong Democrat and an immigration attorney, and, in general, is the kind of voter Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico needs not only to vote for him but to be excited to do so. "My dad worked the railroad, made me go to college, we were LBJ [Lyndon B. Johnson] Democrats, and well, let’s just say, Talarico is obviously very different from Johnson, or even Ann Richards [Texas’ last Democratic governor, who served in the 1990s]." Mark declined to tell me who he was voting for, or even whether he would vote, but I suspect Talarico can count on him, especially given Mark’s less-than-favorable view of Republican Ken Paxton. But there was no excitement when he talked about the race. Like so many others I spoke with, he said, "This isn’t like when Beto [O’Rourke] ran." FOX NEWS POLL: IT’S A LONE STAR SENATE SHOWDOWN BETWEEN TALARICO AND PAXTON If enthusiasm is a potential weak point for the Talarico campaign, then an even more worrisome one is his lagging support in the Black community, long the bedrock of Texas Democratic politics. Jay and Darryl are two Black men in their 50s whom I met while they were having breakfast near the AT&T Discovery District. They each have very different ideas about what is going to happen Tuesday, when voters have their final say. Jay told Fox News Digital of the Senate race, "Actually, I don’t think it's going to be close, he’s going to kill it, because he can get people to flip over," adding, "He would have had a harder time with [Sen. John] Cornyn." Darryl, however, seemed less convinced, arguing that in Texas, "Conservatives aren’t loud, they don’t march, they don’t act up, they paint their hair, but I think they are the silent majority." TALARICO SKIPS BERNIE SANDERS RALLY IN TEXAS, CAMPAIGNS SEPARATELY AS SENATE RACE HEATS UP Both men agreed that Talarico’s failure to mend fences with his primary opponent, Rep. Jasmine Crockett, D-Texas, is a problem for Talarico, but they differed on how significant a problem it was, with Jay arguing, "She’s still helping, just down-ballot." Carlos, who lives in Dallas and works in a hotel, told me over a cigar that looking "at the trajectory of America… I just don’t feel represented in any way." He went on to say, "I really wanted to believe it, the whole thing about no wars… my gas is super expensive from the people who said there was not going to be a war." VOTERS PREPARE TO WEIGH IN ON TRUMP'S ECONOMY AS COSTS CONTINUE TO SURGE This is good news for Talarico, in part because Carlos is a Joe Rogan fan who, though not a President Donald Trump voter, was open to the possibility that Trump could sway him, something that has not happened. On the other side of the ledger for Talarico, or perhaps I should say for Paxton, is Debbie, a suburban mother who told Fox News Digital, "I’m a moderate, I have voted for Democrats, I voted for Beto, but Talarico just says so much crazy stuff, it's too much for Texas." Had these conversations taken place across the Lone Star State, it might be good news for Talarico, but all of these people are in the Dallas area, where he needs to rack up major numbers to offset GOP dominance in rural areas. On Tuesday, I spoke with GOP consultant Vinny Minchillo before we appeared on "The Will Cain Show." He said, "I do not like what I see in the early voting for Paxton." He estimated that the GOP was about 100,000 votes behind but acknowledged that, as a consultant, he never tries to paint a rosy picture. TRUMP WON THIS RELIABLY RED STATE BY DOUBLE DIGITS. NOW A DEADLOCKED RACE IS BRINGING HIM BACK When asked specifically about the early vote in the Black community, he told Fox News Digital, "It looks like it is down." So again, a mixed bag. One wild-card issue that continues to come up in my conversations on the ground is the riots in France, with one voter telling me, "What if that was New York City, or D.C.? That doesn’t really seem impossible." The GOP, especially at Vice President JD Vance’s rallies, has been hitting the France issue and what it says about unchecked immigration, hard in recent days, and I would expect that to continue. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Make no mistake, the Texas Senate race is tight, but if James Talarico cannot shore up the many votes he needs in Big D, it very well could leave Ken Paxton with enough votes in red counties to close the deal with Texas voters and help keep the Senate in Republican hands.

articles.title: In 1957, Kentucky farmer Milton Turner paid $2,500 for a saltwater-mixed oil well; tractor-powered pumping raised its daily output to a month’s former production, helping fuel a local boom
articles.summary: Explore the origins of the Kentucky oil boom initiated by Milton G. Turner in 1957, where innovative pumping techniques transformed abandoned saltwater wells into profitable ventures for farmers like Ellis Hood and Early Vaughn Dulworth, leading to record oil production increases in the state.
articles.body: In 1957, Milton G. Turner purchased an oil well abandoned by Starr Gas Co. upon discovering oil mixed with substantial quantities of salt water. According to Time, Turner had paid $2,500 for the well, along with its equipment, and 80 surrounding acres in Kentucky’s Green County. His approach to pumping the well would go on to usher in the starting point of a wider oil boom. Turner believed that if the water level was lowered quickly enough, it would allow oil to flow from the rock into the bore. By using tractor power to operate a pump, the well in one day produced as much oil as it had produced in a month under Starr’s pumping arrangement.The discovery took place in a region where oil had long been known but had not been developed on a comparable scale. Farmers were aware of oil in a salt-water well dating to 1828, but geologists and oilmen had considered commercial production unfeasible because of the water mixed with the oil.The leases and wells spread across Green CountyThe subsequent lease arrangements that Turner established served to extend a drilling operation beyond his own footprint. TIME reported that Turner had offered leases without charges, as that encouraged others to do the same. Two additional wells came into production during the winter preceding the report, followed in April by a flowing well on the Frank Beams farm along the main Louisville road, when the boom began.The financial benefits of this phenomenon trickled down to landowners whose farms had initially yielded modest returns. One such landowner identified by the report was Ellis Hood, a 45-year-old farmer who worked 85 acres of hilly land and earned $325 a day from the oil activity. Another was a former Marine named Early Vaughn Dulworth, who had paid $200 for a partial interest in the Beams lease and received $2,000 a month. In addition, there was a hamburger-stand operator who was collecting $1,500 a month in royalties on the parking lot after he had leased the stand itself for $15 a month. These instances were ample enough to prove that oil rights and land interests could generate income beyond the direct operation of wells.The same effect was apparent in the lease market, which changed sharply. Agreements that had commanded just $1 per farm and one-eighth of the oil the previous spring rose to $2,500 to $3,000 per acre, with farmers receiving a quarter of the oil.Production records and transport infrastructureIn his review of the 1958 industry, petroleum geologist Edmund Nosow recorded more than 600 wells completed in Green County, which contributed to a statewide drilling total that exceeded 2,300. According to his article titled “Oil and Gas Developments in Kentucky in 1958”, Kentucky’s oil production had totalled 17,956,170 barrels that year. A report just a year later in 1959 showed that Kentucky’s oil production had struck a new record at 27,271,956 barrels, an increase of nearly 52%, while Green and Taylor counties accounted for one-third of the state total.While drilling activity was gaining momentum, at its backdrop, the transport infrastructure had also developed alongside production. TIME reported in December 1958 that Ashland Oil & Refining Co., which purchased much of the field’s output, had invested $200,000 in gathering lines. It was also seeking bids for a $2 million pipeline to its refinery in Louisville, which was approximately 70 miles away. The Kentucky Geological Survey’s historical timeline records that Ashland completed a pipeline from Louisville to the field in 1959 at a cost of approximately $2 million.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2007, a Georgia fatherbegan turningthe tiny villages he made with his eight children into a stone garden of more than 50 miniature castles and cathedrals, now drawing visitors
articles.summary: Discover the enchanting Rock Garden in Calhoun, Georgia, featuring over 50 miniature castles and cathedrals created by DeWitt Boyd for his children. A community hub for reflection and creativity, this unique garden showcases intricate craftsmanship and annual events.
articles.body: There is a miniature world of buildings and places from around the world in a garden behind a church in Calhoun, Georgia. Nestled beside a stream, the garden, also known as “The Rock Garden”, sits just behind the Calhoun Seventh-day Adventist Church on Rome Road. The garden boasts an array of miniature structures that resemble their larger counterparts, and these include several replicas of Paris’s Notre-Dame Cathedral, Japan’s Himeji Castle, and Rome’s Colosseum.The project was set off in 2007, when DeWitt Boyd, a church member known as “Old Dog”, started constructing the garden on the grounds of the church itself. According to Atlas Obscura, Boyd had created these villages as a game for his eight children, giving each child a porcelain figure to represent them in the imaginary settlements, until it eventually emerged as a collection of more than 50 miniature structures.Materials and construction behind the miniature buildingsThrough hits and misses, Boyd created his method of utilising cement reinforced with a long list of materials, including wire, pebbles, shells, broken glass, and ceramic tiles to make the structures. According to a Blue Ridge Country feature on the garden and its builder, the building process demanded both time and strenuous manual effort. It took over 27 months to complete the Notre Dame Cathedral decked with stained glass windows.As per a Roadtrippers report, the garden’s construction methods were passed to volunteers who helped maintain the site. articles.title: California’s 5-foot Mill Creek dam blocked coho for decades; a 2016 fish-passage redesign reopened 11.2 miles, and salmon spawned upstream weeks later
articles.summary: A fish-passage redesign at California's Mill Creek dam opens access to 11.2 miles of stream habitat for endangered coho salmon and steelhead trout, leading to successful spawning just two months after completion.
articles.body: For decades, a five-foot concrete dam on Mill Creek in Sonoma County, California, prevented fish from reaching upstream habitat. The obstruction was addressed in 2016 by a fish-passage project through a redesigned channel, which restored access to 11.2 miles of stream habitat. The dam had restricted fish movement towards upstream stretches that retain water throughout the year, limiting access to spawning and rearing habitat. According to California Sea Grant, after the problems caused by the dam were identified, the NOAA National Marine Fisheries Service deemed it the highest-priority barrier for remediation.Mill Creek is a tributary of the Russian River, west of Healdsburg, and its watershed supports federally endangered coho salmon and threatened steelhead trout. The project formed part of wider efforts to restore the stream's ecological function. Its central objective was to provide fish with passage between the lower creek and the habitat beyond the dam while accommodating the requirements of neighbouring property owners.The redesign combined a roughened ramp with a side channel The engineering solution aimed to modify the existing barrier, adding a new channel around it instead of relying on conventional passage structure alone. According to Prunuske Chatham Inc. (PCI), the construction involved establishing a new channel of approximately 200 feet. This comprised a roughened ramp that led toward the dam crest, followed by a side channel which was excavated around its right-bank abutment.The point of the two routes was to accommodate two different flow conditions of the water that were prevalent at the site. The first challenge was that, at lower flows, water would be concentrated in the side channel. Conversely, the water would pass through both channels when the flows were higher. In response, the main ramp was incorporated with large boulders, smaller stones, cobbles, and gravel, which helped in creating multiple pathways through the structure. In this way, the movement of adult and juvenile salmon was made easier while achieving the site’s specific engineering requirements.Trout Unlimited led implementation of the project and worked side by side with PCI on the design and construction. The project also involved California Sea Grant, UC Cooperative Extension, and public agencies such as the California Department of Fish and Wildlife and the Sonoma County Water Agency. As far as the funding was concerned, it was provided by three agencies: the NOAA Restoration Center's Community-based Restoration Program, the California Department of Fish and Wildlife's Fisheries Restoration Grant Program, and the Sonoma County Water Agency.Post-construction monitoring documented upstream spawning In October 2016, the construction of the main and side channels was completed, and follow-up biological monitoring of the region showed that coho salmon spawned above the former dam site. Considering the fact that this happened weeks after the work was completed, this was a very substantial change. On top of that, before the remediation, coho salmon had only been recorded spawning in the lower reaches of Mill Creek.California Sea Grant’s habitat enhancement monitoring programme kept track of the changes through surveys which were conducted before and after the remediation. As per their record, spawning showed increased activity above the former barrier during the winters once the construction had been completed. This was enough to discern that the redesigned passage has restored access to habitat which had been previously inaccessible.More signs of the resurgence of fish were recorded by the Trout Unlimited project in March 2017, which showed that more than eight coho salmon redds, or nests, were present upstream of the project site that year. For the assessment, both physical conditions at the site and biological evidence were considered, including adult spawning activity and juvenile fish use. The results demonstrated that a targeted modification to a longstanding obstruction could reconnect a substantial length of stream habitat.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: A Norfolk farming couple spent £1.5 million fighting to protect a wetland; after 15 years and three legal victories, a court ruled that regulators had failed to prevent pollution threatening 2,500 species
articles.summary: A conservation battle in England’s Norfolk Broads has resulted in another significant legal victory for two farmers who have spent years challenging
articles.body: A conservation battle in England’s Norfolk Broads has resulted in another significant legal victory for two farmers who have spent years challenging authorities over the protection of a rare wetland. As reported by The Guardian and the High Court judgment in Harris v Natural England, Tim and Geli Harris have won their third major legal case after the High Court found that Natural England had failed to fulfil its legal responsibilities to protect Catfield Fen from pollution. Coverage of the case highlights broader concerns about environmental oversight, agricultural runoff and the difficulties of holding public agencies accountable for damage to sensitive ecosystems. The couple, who own a 460-acre farm in the Norfolk Broads, have spent around £1.5 million of their own money pursuing legal action over 15 years. Their campaign centres on Catfield Fen, a wetland of international conservation importance that supports approximately 2,500 species, including rare orchids, ferns, breeding bitterns and swallowtail butterflies.Why Catfield Fen is under threatCatfield Fen is part of a legally protected Special Area of Conservation within the Broads, a landscape known for its distinctive waterways, wetlands and wildlife. Its ecological health depends on a delicate balance of water levels and nutrient conditions, making it particularly vulnerable to changes in groundwater supplies and pollution.The latest court ruling concerns nitrates and phosphates entering the wetland from surrounding agricultural land. These nutrients can disrupt the natural balance of sensitive habitats, encouraging excessive plant and algal growth and threatening species adapted to nutrient-poor conditions.The High Court found that Natural England had failed in its statutory duty to protect the site. The decision followed the couple’s efforts to bring the pollution problem to the regulator’s attention, with the judge criticising the agency’s failure to take adequate action. The ruling adds to longstanding concerns about whether environmental protections are being enforced effectively, even when vulnerable habitats have formal legal safeguards.Three legal victories over 15 yearsThe latest judgment is the third major success in the Harrises’ prolonged campaign to protect the fen. Their first significant victory came in 2016, following a public inquiry that established that excessive groundwater extraction by water companies and local farmers was contributing to the wetland drying out. Water abstraction can lower groundwater levels, disrupting the conditions that sustain fen vegetation and wildlife.In 2022, the couple secured another legal victory that forced the Environment Agency to restrict water abstraction near other ecologically important sites in the Norfolk Broads. Their latest case shifts attention towards pollution from agricultural land and Natural England’s responsibility to protect the habitat. Together, the three victories have exposed different pressures affecting the same landscape: declining water availability, nutrient pollution and weaknesses in environmental enforcement.The cases also illustrate how different public bodies may have overlapping responsibilities for protecting a single ecosystem, while effective intervention can depend on sustained monitoring and coordinated action.A farming model built around conservationThe Harrises bought their farm in 1994, drawn by the opportunity to live closer to nature. Since then, they have converted arable fields into pasture to reduce the risk of soil and agricultural runoff reaching the fen. Their land management includes caring for English White Park cattle, sheep and rare-breed Eriskay ponies. The couple also maintain the wetland through carefully managed vegetation cutting designed to preserve its plants and wildlife. Their conservation work has, however, put them at odds with some fellow farmers.Restrictions on groundwater extraction can affect agricultural production, particularly water-intensive crops such as potatoes. The couple have said their position is not intended to oppose farming, but to ensure that agricultural activity does not undermine the natural systems on which the wider landscape depends. Despite improvements in water levels and biodiversity in parts of the wetland since the 2022 ruling, they remain concerned about declining insect numbers and the possibility that pollution continues to go undetected elsewhere.What happens next?The court is expected to issue further rulings setting out what Natural England must do to address pollution at Catfield Fen. The Harrises believe one practical measure would be to establish grassland buffer strips between cultivated fields and drainage ditches, helping prevent nutrient-rich soil from washing into waterways.They have also called for environmental regulators to devote greater resources to monitoring and enforcing existing rules. Without adequate oversight, breaches may continue without timely detection or intervention. Natural England has accepted the court’s finding that it did not do enough to protect the wetland, although it has declined to comment further while legal proceedings continue.The couple do not want their remaining years to be consumed by litigation. Nevertheless, they are considering further action over pollution in the Broads. Their daughter is expected to continue managing the farm, extending the family’s involvement in conservation beyond the current legal battles.The case serves as a reminder that legal protection alone cannot guarantee the survival of threatened habitats. Protecting wetlands requires effective regulation, consistent enforcement and cooperation between agriculture, government agencies and conservationists. For Catfield Fen, the latest ruling marks another step forward, but the long-term recovery of its wildlife will depend on what happens after the courtroom battle ends.You use AI every day. articles.title: Meet Rick Senko, 41, the Florida single father who flipped a $35 cellphone for $70 on eBay in 2008; today, his pre-owned clothing business sells $40 Burberry coats and generates $6.5 million a year
articles.summary: Rick Senko was unemployed, broke and raising his five-year-old son alone when a broken cellphone changed his life.
articles.body: Rick Senko was unemployed, broke and raising his five-year-old son alone when a broken cellphone changed his life. In 2008, with few job opportunities available, he bought a replacement phone on Craigslist for $35 and listed it on eBay for $70. It sold the same day, giving him his first glimpse of the money-making potential of reselling.Nearly two decades later, the 41-year-old entrepreneur from South Florida has built a multimillion-dollar business selling pre-owned clothing. According to CNBC Make It, Senko generated $6.5 million in sales in 2024, turning his knack for finding bargains into a thriving wholesale operation.But his journey from an unemployed single father to a successful entrepreneur has involved years of relentless work, early mornings and personal sacrifices.How a broken cellphone sparked a multimillion-dollar businessSenko grew up in South Florida with a single mother who worked as a waitress at Denny's. He became a father at 18, and by 2008, he was struggling to find employment amid the economic downturn. With a young son to support and little money to spare, he began looking for alternative ways to earn a living.When his cellphone broke, he went on eBay to check the cost of a replacement. That led to an idea that would eventually shape his career: buying an item at a lower price and selling it for a profit."I had the bright idea to go onto Craigslist, buy the phone for $35, list it on eBay for $70, and it sold the same day for $70," Senko told CNBC Make It."That was a light bulb moment, and I've been doing that ever since for almost 20 years. Rinse and repeat."He initially focused on electronics before gradually moving into pre-owned clothing. What began as a way to make ends meet eventually became a full-fledged business built around identifying undervalued products and finding buyers willing to pay more for them.From flea market bargains to high-end designer clothingSenko's business relies on spotting valuable items where others might see unwanted goods. His search often begins at flea markets, where he arrives before sunrise to get first pick of the merchandise.During CNBC Make It's visit, he demonstrated how seemingly ordinary finds can translate into substantial profits. A vintage Abercrombie & Fitch item purchased for $10, for instance, could sell for around $100 or more. He also showed two Burberry trench coats bought for $40 apiece, estimating that one could fetch $250 to $300 and the other around $200.The challenge lies in knowing what to buy, how much to pay and whether an item is authentic. Senko examines labels, logos and other identifying details to distinguish genuine products from counterfeits, a particularly important skill when dealing with sought-after brands.For him, the flea market is more than a place to shop. It is an ecosystem of small businesses, each with its own specialisation and customer base."Everyone's here looking for deals," he said, describing the people who come to the market to source products for resale.He also believes that making a profit should not come at the expense of the people supplying the merchandise. Explaining why he sometimes pays more than the lowest possible price, he said, "We all gotta make some money."He added that if sellers stopped earning enough to return to the market, his own business would suffer too.How he became eBay's leading seller of pre-owned men's clothingSenko's persistence helped him scale beyond individual transactions. He said he eventually became eBay's number one seller in pre-owned men's clothing, building a substantial online operation.Recalling the peak of his eBay business on April 14, 2021, he said the operation was generating around $2.5 million annually, with approximately 50,000 items listed in the store and 100,000 items sold each year.He attributes that growth to consistency rather than a single breakthrough."I believe it was a lot of tenacity and I had a lot of consistency," he said. "And every single day I woke up and I did my job to the best of my ability."Over time, however, his business model evolved again. Rather than selling every item individually to consumers, he moved into wholesale, supplying other resellers who then process, list and sell the products themselves.Inside his $6.5 million resale businessBy 2024, Senko's business was generating $6.5 million in annual sales. His wholesale operation supplies other resellers with large volumes of pre-owned merchandise, including clothing, shoes, accessories and even video game collections.He said customers order directly from him, with the operation processing roughly 1,000 pieces a week for resale. The scale of the business reflects how far he has moved from buying and flipping a single cellphone.Senko also expects the business to grow further. Speaking to CNBC Make It, he said he anticipated considerably higher sales in 2025, although the interview excerpt does not provide a final figure for that year.The business also highlights the amount of usable merchandise that is discarded in the United States. Senko said he regularly comes across designer scarves, premium clothing and other branded items that might otherwise end up in the trash."I think you understand very quickly the amount of waste that's in the United States of America when people are discarding Hermes scarves," he said."Because if we didn't get it, it would have been in the trash."By finding new buyers for these products, his business gives pre-owned goods another chance at being used while creating an income stream for the resellers who purchase them.'I have never taken a day off in almost 20 years'For all the impressive sales figures, Senko's story is also one of relentless work. He said he has not taken a day off in nearly two decades, a commitment he connects directly to the opportunities that reselling has given him."I have never taken a day off in almost 20 years. Never. How much? I get after it every single day," he said.He explained that once someone understands how a small investment can multiply into a much larger amount, it becomes difficult to switch off from the pursuit."When you unlock the power that this is, the ability to multiply money to take $5, put it onto eBay and sell something and get $25 back. How in the world can you rest? I don't get it," he said.His drive also comes from experiences within his family. Senko recalled that his grandfather stopped working and died two weeks later, an event that left a lasting impression on him.He suggested that the experience reinforced his instinct to keep moving forward rather than stop working.The sacrifices behind his successSenko is candid that building a business of this size has required far more than an ability to spot bargains. Reflecting on his journey, he said the transformation from being broke and unemployed to running a multimillion-dollar operation came with considerable demands on his time and personal life."It also took a tremendous amount of work, a tremendous amount of commitment, and a tremendous amount of sacrifice to get from where I came from to now selling millions of dollars per year and living a very, very fortunate life," he said.You use AI every day.
