articles.title: Israel's election deadlock is a sign of the country's deep divisions
articles.summary: The election was a celebration of democracy in some ways - but it has left Israel with no clear path to a new government, writes James Landale.
articles.body:
"Democracy is the worst form of government except for all those other forms that have been tried." So said Winston Churchill in the House of Commons in 1947.

His aphorism came to mind as Israel's election results filtered through on Tuesday night - exit polls blending with ballots that were cast to dash or fulfil people's hopes and fears.

This election has, in some ways, been a celebration of democracy. Voters turning out in record numbers, Jews and Arabs alike. Many spent thousands to fly in from abroad to cast their ballot.

At polling stations across the country, we saw the passion of campaigners, as they used every minute to try to change that last mind and win that last vote.

President Isaac Herzog said the election was a "badge of honour" for Israeli society. "It is remarkable to see how deep the desire for democracy is in Israel," he exclaimed.

Yet this election left the most established democracy in the Middle East without a clear path to a new government. It produced an inconclusive result where neither opposing bloc will have a majority in parliament.

Some might say this was business as usual.

Israel has never had a one-party government. Its fragmented, proportional representation system is almost designed to govern by coalition.

Yet many commentators warned this election had revealed the fundamental and perhaps growing divisions that scar this nation. This was not a plebiscite in which an electorate united around a single cause.

Some of these fissures are not new. There were divisions over judicial reforms that led to mass demonstrations in the early years of this government.

There were also divisions over how to respond to the deadly 7 October 2023 attacks - whether to save hostages or destroy Hamas. The casualties suffered by Israeli reservists in the fighting in Gaza that followed deepened tensions over the exemption of ultra-Orthodox young men from military service .

But has this election put in even sharper contrast the deep fault-lines that lie within Israeli society?

There are the tensions between the religious and the secular, divides not just of faith but of society.

Should Israel's government subsidise religious study? Should some parents sacrifice their sons and daughters to defend Israel when others do not? The ultra-Orthodox now make up almost 15% of the population. Their world-view is poles apart from that of denizens of high-tech, modern neighbourhoods of Tel Aviv.

There are divisions over fundamental politics.

Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party suffered significant losses, but is still on track to be the largest in the Knesset. All this for a prime minister accused of corruption, which he denies; a leader also accused of failing to protect Israel before 7 October, something he will not allow to be investigated .

Some 10% of voters backed the Jewish supremacist far-right: politicians like Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, who even as results were being announced was promising to establish Jewish settlements in Gaza.

The Arab parties, which represent about a fifth of Israeli citizens, made huge gains, winning some 15% of the vote, potentially giving them seats numbering in the high teens.

And then there was the opposition bloc, a mix of centre, left and right led by Gadi Eisenkot who fell short of winning the change they wanted - change that many believed was existential for the future of this country.

How these vastly diverging views coalesce into some form of government is now the unenviable task facing Israel's body politic - the choices and compromises they may have to make could involve fundamental decisions about the country's future.

Would Netanyahu be ready to abandon his religious allies and form a coalition with right-wingers from the opposition bloc? Would they be ready to swallow their hostility towards the prime minister and sit in his government?

Is the opposition bloc ready to abandon much of its campaign promises and co-operate with Arab parties to force Netanyahu out of office? Are the Arab parties ready to risk joining a government that could fall within months?

Yair Golan, the left-wing Democrat leader, urged the opposition bloc to form a partnership with Arab parties. "We must no longer accept Netanyahu's racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes," he said.

But are the people of Israel ready for such a reality?

Amit Segal, an Israeli commentator sympathetic towards Netanyahu, said the high turnout among Arab Israeli voters "reminded Jews on both sides that, after years of division, they may have to learn to sit together after all".

The risk is that this election, instead of putting Israel on a new path, has instead raised further doubts about what it is that unites its citizens. What are the common factors that bind this complex, varied collection of peoples into one polity?

Autocratic governments, which are growing in number, have long criticised democracies for producing weak and temporary governments, often fragile coalitions that struggle to hold together, let alone deliver what the people wanted.

Israel may now struggle for months to form a government. It might even fail and have to hold another election.

President Herzog acknowledged this risk head on as he prepared to open coalition negotiations: "We must do everything we can, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections."

For years, Israel has focused on defending itself against its external enemies. But must it also now be ready to defend itself from perils within, if the divisions writ large by this election become unmanageable?

In another speech, Churchill once said democracy was not just "insurance against dangers from abroad". It was also, he added, "insurance against dangers scarcely less grave and much more near and constant which threaten us here at home".

Can Israel's democracy live up to this challenge?

articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Delhi high court on Wednesday dismissed a PIL challenging the central govt’s decision to increase passport fees for non-resident Indians
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Delhi high court on Wednesday dismissed a PIL challenging the central govt’s decision to increase passport fees for non-resident Indians (NRIs), observing that a 67% hike after a gap of 14 years is not “unreasonable or exorbitant”. Acting chief justice Nitin Wasudeo Sambre and justice Sanjay Sharma added that the decision to determine the fees falls within the policy domain of the govt and judicial intervention was not warranted.Pravasi Legal Cell filed the petition, alleging discrimination against NRIs, who are required to pay around Rs 11,900 for passports, compared to Rs 2,500 for resident Indians.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Massachusetts town can take conservation and beach access rights over Northeastern University land despite plans for campus expansion, high court rules
articles.summary: The Supreme Judicial Court of Massachusetts has ruled that the town of Nahant can take conservation and public access easements over land owned by
articles.body: The Supreme Judicial Court of Massachusetts has ruled that the town of Nahant can take conservation and public access easements over land owned by Northeastern University, despite the effect on the university’s planned campus expansion. In Town of Nahant v. Northeastern University, decided on September 3, 2026, the state’s highest court reversed a lower court ruling that had found the town’s stated public purpose to be a pretext for stopping development. The dispute concerns East Point, a coastal peninsula where Northeastern operates a Marine Science Center and the town maintains a public park. Nahant’s plan would restrict development across about 12.5 acres and establish public access to Canoe Beach. The court held that conservation, open space and scenic preservation are legitimate public purposes under Massachusetts law, and that Northeastern had no reasonable chance of proving the taking invalid on grounds of bad faith. The case returns to the Superior Court, which is to enter an order establishing the town’s right to take the easements. The town must still pay just compensation.East Point dispute: why Nahant sought conservation and access easements over Northeastern University landEast Point is a 28.7-acre peninsula in Nahant, a small coastal town in Essex County, Massachusetts. Northeastern owns 20.4 acres of the peninsula, including the site of its Marine Science Center, while the town owns the remaining 8.3 acres, which it maintains as a public park. Access to the park crosses university property under an existing easement. In 2018, Northeastern announced plans to expand its campus at East Point. The proposal included a 55,000-square-foot building, additional parking and a geothermal wellfield. The plans prompted opposition from residents and town officials concerned about development in the area. In May 2021, town meeting voted to authorise the use of eminent domain to acquire conservation and public access easements over university land. The votes approved the taking and the use of $1.5 million in Community Preservation Act funds to help pay for it. The town’s board of selectmen subsequently issued an order covering two conservation easements and one access easement across roughly 12 acres.The conservation easements would preserve the land in an open condition and prevent new buildings, while allowing existing structures to be used and maintained. The access easement would establish public rights to use Canoe Beach for outdoor recreation. The Nahant Preservation Trust, a nonprofit organisation, donated $3 million earmarked for the taking under a gift agreement. Nahant petitioned the Massachusetts Superior Court to establish its right to acquire the easements. Northeastern challenged the action, arguing that conservation was not the town’s true objective and that the taking was intended to stop its planned expansion. The Superior Court agreed with the university, dismissed the town’s petition and awarded Northeastern more than $1 million in attorney’s fees and costs. The town appealed.Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court ruling: why conservation and scenic protection qualify as public purposesThe Supreme Judicial Court examined whether Nahant’s stated reasons for taking the easements amounted to a legitimate public purpose. Justice Dewar, writing for the court, explained that public-purpose determinations give substantial weight to legislative judgment, and that courts generally do not investigate the motives of individual voters behind a town’s formal decision. The court said preserving land in a natural, scenic and open condition is a recognised public purpose. Article 97 of the Massachusetts Constitution expressly identifies the protection of natural resources as a public purpose, while earlier court decisions have recognised scenic preservation as a legitimate objective as well. Northeastern argued that protecting the town’s scenic character was insufficient to justify the taking. The justices rejected that argument, relying on Massachusetts precedent and the broader principles governing eminent domain, the legal power of government to acquire private property for public use subject to compensation.The university also argued that the Dover Amendment, which limits the extent to which local zoning rules can restrict certain educational uses of land, should prevent Nahant from using eminent domain to interfere with its planned campus development. The court disagreed. It noted that the Massachusetts Legislature had imposed specific restrictions on eminent domain involving certain categories of land but had not created a comparable restriction for property used for educational purposes. The ruling does not mean the town can acquire the easements without paying the university. The court stressed that Nahant must provide Northeastern with just compensation for the property rights taken.Pheasant Ridge test: why the court found insufficient evidence of bad faithThe central dispute concerned whether the town was using conservation as a pretext to block Northeastern’s development. In Pheasant Ridge Associates Limited Partnership v. Burlington, a 1987 Massachusetts decision, the court established that a municipality cannot use eminent domain solely to prevent a development while disguising that objective behind a purported public purpose. Northeastern pointed to statements by officials and residents opposing its expansion, suggestions that the taking could be used as leverage, and the fact that the town began pursuing eminent domain after the university announced its plans. It argued that these circumstances showed the conservation rationale was not genuine.The Supreme Judicial Court found the evidence insufficient to establish a viable bad-faith challenge. The town’s interest in preserving East Point predated the 2018 development proposal. Nahant had established its public park there in 1986, and the university’s land was placed in a natural-resource zoning district in 1991. Town open-space plans also identified the area as valuable for recreation and wildlife. The court considered the town’s decision-making process, including the formal town-meeting procedure, financial review and public debate. It also noted that the proposed easements were designed around the stated conservation and access goals and that the land already lay in a zoning district intended to protect open space.Because a conservation easement necessarily restricts development, the fact that the taking would prevent Northeastern’s proposed building did not, by itself, establish bad faith. The court also held that a taking serving a public purpose is not invalid merely because a private party supports it financially or advocates for it. The justices concluded that Northeastern had no reasonable expectation of proving the taking invalid under the applicable legal standard. They reversed the Superior Court’s judgment, including its award of attorney’s fees and costs, and remanded the case for entry of an order establishing the town’s right to take the property interests described in its order of intention, along with further proceedings. The decision resolves the key legal challenge to Nahant’s stated public purpose. The Superior Court is to enter the required order, while the remaining proceedings include determining the compensation owed to Northeastern. The town must pay just compensation for the easements it acquires.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: The definitive fast-casual sit-down restaurant Mount Rushmore in the wake of 'CheesecakeGate'
articles.summary: From Olive Garden's endless breadsticks to Chili's Three-For-Me deals, this Mount Rushmore of fast-casual sit-down restaurants sparked debate.
articles.body: I was on vacation in Chicago this past week, and while I try to stay up to date on current events as much as I can when I'm out, that usually just equates to me watching a ton of college football and forgetting the outside world exists. Last week was no different, and when I got back home on Monday night and started to shift back into "OutKick mode," I saw the fine dining establishment known as the Cheesecake Factory was trending on social media. I felt pretty out of the loop, but after seeing people pick a side of the aisle to fall on in the Great Cheesecake Factory Debate as well as rank some of their other favorite sit-down restaurants, I knew it was time to throw my hat in the ring. BABY BOOMERS CROWN THEIR FAVORITE CASUAL DINING CHAIN AS GEN Z CHOOSES A DIFFERENT WINNER If there are three things you must know about me, it's that I'm passionate about sports, music and eating at restaurants. That might come as a shock to anyone who has seen me in person, considering I'm about 160lbs soaking wet and looked like an emaciated child until I was 25 years old, but I am a chain restaurant connoisseur of sorts. With all the commotion surrounding the Cheesecake Factory, and American eateries as a whole, I thought now would be as good a time as any to share my Mount Rushmore of fast-casual sit-down restaurants. AMERICA'S FAVORITE FAST-FOOD CHAIN NAMED: MCDONALD'S WINS HEARTS BUT NOT BEST BURGER, SURVEY SAYS This isn't just some slapped together list either (shout out to "Rolling Stone"), as this topic is something that I'm constantly revisiting and reevaluating. This Mount Rushmore represents a good mix of four different kinds of food and dining experiences, with different menus, atmospheres, and themes. With all the preamble out of the way, let's begin. Olive Garden We start this list off with a bang, and a somewhat controversial one at that. I'm not sure why Olive Garden has this reputation as a classless knockoff (my dad calls it the McDonald's of Italian food), but I would never slander a place that offers endless breadsticks and pasta. The soups are incredible, the variety of pastas is awesome, and the entrées are varied and filling. BELOVED RESTAURANT CHAIN DWINDLES FROM 850 LOCATIONS TO 87, BUT EXPERT SEES 'A LOT OF LIFE LEFT' The vibes are immaculate too, giving me a classy place to "sample The Boot." My go-to choice is the chicken parm (duh), but I've never had a bad meal at Olive Garden and I don't plan on it anytime soon. Texas Roadhouse If you're looking for good old American fare at solid prices, look no further than Texas Roadhouse. Their steaks are some of the best you can get at their price point, and the ability to smother them in sautéed onions and mushrooms is underrated. Texas Roadhouse isn't just a one-trick pony, though, as their appetizers — the cheese fries in particular — are immaculate, and their chili is some of the best in the biz. I know what you all are here for, and I would be remiss if I didn't mention the bread rolls, which would probably merit placement on this list by themselves. They really lean into their Texas themes here, too, and if you've ever had a birthday at Roadhouse, you know exactly what I'm talking about. Can I get a "yeehaw?" Chuy's Maybe it's just because I lived in Dallas for six years, but TexMex is supremely underrated and should be more of a national delicacy. Luckily, Chuy's is a national TexMex chain that is worthy of both Lone Star State natives and outsiders alike. Their signature sauces go with just about any of their entrées, and although I'm not a big drinker, I have to say that their frozen margarita machines are worth the price of admission alone. Whether you're into spice or just some good old-fashioned, hearty fare from the southwest, Chuy's has you covered. The biggest selling point, to me though, is the creamy jalapeño ranch dip they give you with your chips and salsa. Every great sit-down restaurant has a "gimmick," and this one is undeniably delicious. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! It's the perfect blend of creamy ranch and spice that will have you filling up on chips before your meal even comes out. Chili's For my money, there is no greater fast-casual sit-down establishment in this great country than Chili's. The menu is insanely diverse. You can get seafood alfredo, steak, southwestern salad and traditional American fare all on a single page. CHILI'S GOES VIRAL AFTER ROASTING FAST-FOOD PRICES: 'WHY LET THEM PLAY YOU LIKE THIS?' Their lunch deals are also second to none, with the Three-For-Me and Three-For-$10 being go-to's for yours truly. There is nothing better than sitting in the Chili's bar on a college football Saturday afternoon, ordering some chips and salsa and an ice-cold Coke and just soaking in the ambience. My personal favorite has to be the Chipotle Fresh Mex Bowl, but I've been known to get a classic sirloin, the Margarita Grilled Chicken, or even the boneless wings, which are incredible even though I'm normally a traditionalist when it comes to wings. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP I could write an entire book on my love for Chili's, but this has gone on long enough and my mouth is starting to water, so if you'll excuse me, I think I hear a Triple Dipper calling my name.

articles.title: German wolf attack: Girl seriously injured at wildlife park
articles.summary: The eight-year-old was in an enclosure with other children and a staff member when she was attacked.
articles.body:
An eight-year-old girl has been seriously injured in a wolf attack at a German wildlife park.

She was inside an enclosure at the Johannismühle park in Brandenburg, south of Berlin, with a staff member and two other children when the attack happened, police said.

They said in a statement that the "precise circumstances of the incident are the subject of an ongoing police investigation".

The girl was taken to hospital by helicopter after the incident on Wednesday. No one else was injured.

The park, in the town of Baruth/Mark, has been closed temporarily and is set to reopen on 2 November, according to its website, which did not give further details.

The park keeps grey and arctic wolves, along with other animals including the brown bear and lynx.

The girl was injured by at least one animal and suffered head injuries, according to German newspaper Bild.

It reported that the incident happened before the park opened at 10:00 local time (09:00 GMT) and that the girl could have been taking part in a special visit.

Johannismühle offers small group tours to allow visitors to spend time with some animals, with its site mentioning feeding wolves or petting a llama.

The incident comes after a number of other animal attacks at zoos and wildlife parks in Europe.

A keeper at a Dutch zoo died this week after being mauled by a leopard, and a man was killed by a tiger at Yorkshire Wildlife Park earlier this month.

articles.title: Details of thousands of US immigration agents leaked in major hack
articles.summary: A group called the Department of Peace released information on more than 41,000 DHS staff.
articles.body:
Details of more than 41,000 personnel working for the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), including thousands involved in immigration enforcement, have been leaked to the public.

The leak includes names, work addresses, and phone numbers of DHS staff, including agents working with Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection, along with descriptions of the work that they do for each agency.

Wednesday's leak marks the third time in recent weeks that a government agency has been targeted in leaks or hacks.

A representative of the DHS did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The seemingly unprecedented breach of employee information was put online on Wednesday by a group called the Department of Peace alongside cybersecurity researcher and hacker maia crimew.

The information was put in a database named Icepick and shared through a website hosted by Distributed Denial of Secrets.

The groups wrote in an online statement that the goal of the leak was not meant to be a directory of every DHS agent. Rather the aim was to replace "anonymity with accountability", according to Emma Best, a co founder of DDoSecrets.

"The leak is extraordinary but deceptive in it's simplicity as it identifies the officials responsible for overseeing covert and undercover operations, the government's hunt for leakers and the failed BlueLeaks investigation - along with key personnel in DHS's ever-escalating rendition and deportation programs," Best added.

The Department of Peace said on Wednesday that it accessed the DHS agent profiles through a single sign-on service called Okta.

Okta is a popular online security tool that organisations use to ensure that only people with access to internal platforms are logging on to them.

A spokeswoman for Okta said the company is aware of the claims being made, but said: "Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised."

Last month, the FBI was hacked with a group called ShinyHunters taking personal information about thousands of agents.

In recent days, the Federal Election Commission, which makes public political campaign donation data, was taken offline because of a suspected hacking attempt.
